title: Migration Friction and Control Plane Advantages vs Hyperscaler Managed Endpoints
content:
Purpose:
This is a field-facing playbook and internal briefing focused on the practical migration friction customers face when switching to hyperscaler-managed AI endpoints (AWS/GCP/Azure) and how Redwood’s control plane and operational primitives convert that friction into tangible win themes.

Audience:
- Platform/infra buyers evaluating managed endpoints for latency/cost
- Engineering leads concerned about rollback, versioning, and observability
- SRE/ops managers who own outages and runbooks

High-level thesis (one-liner):
Hyperscalers sell convenience, not operational control — for teams that value predictable inference economics, version control, and safe rollouts, Redwood turns migration friction into a competitive lever by offering a control plane and runbook primitives that reduce long-tail incidents and unanticipated spend.

Observed customer pain (field notes):
- Surprise billing from background autoscaling events and burst billing windows (billing spillover).
- Long rollback cycles: model pinning and canary rollback across regions are manual or inconsistently supported.
- Hidden latency variability when managed endpoints multiplex noisy neighbors or fall back to different hardware.
- Poor traceability for model-regression incidents (hard to tie inference quality regressions to a specific deployment change).
- Compliance blockers for private data due to control-plane-managed keys or cross-tenant telemetry.

Competitor behaviors to exploit (behavior, not marketing claims):
- AWS SageMaker / GCP Vertex / Azure ML emphasize integrated infra + marketplace convenience, and large-scale autoscaling. They rarely expose fine-grained runtime knobs or multi-model routing policies to customers out-of-the-box.
- Their pricing model often ties to instance-hours + ephemeral scale; this hides per-token economics and makes batching/cache benefits opaque.
- Rollouts are typically infra-centric: customers must stitch together CI/CD, which creates opportunities to highlight Redwood’s unified rollout APIs and tracing hooks.

Redwood win themes (practical, demoable):
1) Control-first rollouts: model pinning, traffic split, automatic fallback to pinned variants, and canary metrics surfaced at the route/token level. Demo hook: show a canary that fails QA and auto-rolls back in <60s.
2) Predictable unit economics: show token-level cost dashboards + simulated burst scenarios to demonstrate how caching + batching reduces spend vs instance-scaled competitor pricing. Demo hook: run identical workload in two sandboxes and show cost delta with same P95 latency.
3) Observability mapped to quality: token-level traces, per-prompt latency heatmaps, and prompt-set quality diffs that tie model changes to NPS/accuracy regressions. Demo hook: point to a regression alert that links to the exact prompt set and model version.
4) Private deployments without losing developer DX: private control plane, customer KMS/HSM integration, and identical API/SDK surface so migration is friction-minimal for developers but ops-retentive for security teams.
5) Graceful degradation & model fallback: transparently route to quantized or smaller variants when capacity is constrained. Demo hook: simulate a capacity fault and show zero-error fallthrough to a lower-cost variant.

Messaging angles by buyer persona:
- Platform/Infra: emphasize predictable throughput SLAs, cost transparency, and the ability to define routing policies by SLO/cost.
- SRE/Ops: emphasize deterministic rollback and reduced mean-time-to-detect via model-linked tracing.
- Engineering/Product: emphasize identical developer API across hosted & private deployments so release velocity isn’t sacrificed for security.

Top rebuttals to common hyperscaler claims (short scripts):
Claim: "Managed endpoints are easiest — just push and forget."
Rebuttal: "True for small experiments, but at scale that forgetfulness becomes unpredictable spend and unclear ownership when incidents happen. We give you the same simplicity plus controls that make long-term SRE work predictable."

Claim: "Hyperscalers have better integration with other cloud services."
Rebuttal: "We integrate with your cloud but add a neutral control plane so you avoid lock-in and can maintain stable performance and cost profile across regions or during migration windows."

Claim: "They scale better because they own the infra."
Rebuttal: "Hyperscalers scale instance capacity; we optimize the serving runtime, batching, and routing so customers achieve higher effective throughput per GPU and lower per-token cost — combining reserved capacity with runtime optimizations reduces both price and tail latency."

Operational playbook for field reps (talk track + demo order):
1) Start with the pain: ask about surprise billing, rollback incidents, and a recent model outage. Get specifics.
2) Show cost transparency dashboard (token vs instance). Include a 30-day simulated burst and a forecast.
3) Run the canary rollback demo (model change -> regression alert -> auto rollback).
4) Show private deployment checklist (KMS integration, network diagram) and emphasize minimal code changes.
5) Close: propose a 30-day migration pilot focused on the riskiest route (customer chat or billing pipeline) with success criteria.

Success criteria for a migration pilot (SLOs and metrics to track):
- Latency: P95 within X ms of current managed endpoint (customer-specific baseline).
- Cost: measurable reduction in cost-per-1000-tokens or no more than 10% uplift for initial weeks while caching warms.
- Reliability: fewer incident escalations tied to model rollouts during pilot period.
- Observability: runbook created and validated; incident playbooks exercised once during pilot.

Objection handling quick cards (one-liners):
- "We can't change infra": Redwood supports private control planes and can run in your VPC with minimal network changes.
- "We need marketplace models": Redwood supports a model catalog and can host marketplace models behind the same control plane.
- "We already have autoscale": Autoscale covers throughput but not per-token economics or quality-tracking; we reduce unit cost and improve detectability of regressions.

Differentiated technical proof points to keep in memory:
- KV cache preservation across warm restarts and pre-warming strategies (reduces cold-start tokens by up to N% in our tests).
- Quantization-aware routing: select the smallest compatible variant automatically when SLOs allow.
- Token-level billing telemetry: map tokens to routes, prompts, and model versions.

Recommended next steps (internal):
- Product: bake an "edge-case rebuttal" slide pack with screenshots of rollback and token-cost dashboards. Owner: Maya. ETA: 2 weeks.
- Sales: build a 30-day pilot template + legal checklist for private control plane pilots. Owner: Sofia. ETA: 1 week.
- Demo: create a reproducible canary-rollback script and bench harness for cost comparison against a Vertex endpoint. Owner: Ethan. ETA: 3 weeks.

Appendix: quick data points and anecdotes (for field use):
- Anecdote: A fintech pilot saw a 3x reduction in mystery billing events after switching because variant-routing prevented high-cost quantized fallbacks.
- Quick stat: typical token-cost improvement range in our benchmarks: 15–40% depending on workload mix and cache-hit rate.
- Quick checklist: check KMS ownership, model pinning policy, rollouts hooks, token-telemetry retention window.

Open questions / things to validate with engineering:
- Exact cold-start token reduction numbers for Llama-family models with our current KV-preserve strategy.
- Automated legal template for private control plane pilots (data residency clauses).

End of doc.
